title: Who did I miss? #broadway #theatre #playwright #offbroadway
transcript: Who do you think is the most significant and accomplished American theatre writer whose work has never been done on Broadway? I feel like since we've come back from the theatre shutdowns in 2021, we've seen a big influx of major writers making their Broadway debut, both in terms of contemporary writers and also ones from the canon, like Adrienne Kennedy and Alice Childress. So now I'm wondering, like, who's left? Who are either the most significant and influential or the most popular American theater writers whose work has still never been done on Broadway? My first guest that came to mind was Maria Irene Fornes, but actually, she did have a show on Broadway once, a play called The Office that closed in 1966 after 10 previews before officially opening. I think a really big one would be Amiri Baraka, maybe most known for writing the play Dutchman, which has actually been adapted into movie twice. On the more contemporary side, I feel like the two biggest ones would be Lauren Gunderson and Annie Baker. I feel like Annie Baker has been massively influential in contemporary playwriting, and people constantly use her distinct style as a reference point of comparison. And Lauren Gunderson, famously *the* most produced playwright around the country, but very rarely is her work performed in New York. Now her work has been performed in New York, but never on Broadway. I also tried to think who on the musical theatre side would fit this description. And I had trouble thinking of anyone, but I landed on maybe Adam Gwon. Not only is he a very accomplished musical theatre writer, but, of course, his songs have become a staple of cabarets, auditions, etc. He's definitely cemented his foothold in the canon of American musical theater. And of course, I have to mention, not all of these artists maybe want to have their work done on Broadway. Especially someone like Annie Baker, whose work is famously very quiet and intimate, you know, like, she might not want that. I'm not using this as, like, a metric for success. I just think it's interesting.
